title: How to Calculate Your True Close Rate (Most Owners Get This Wrong)
excerpt: Most owners calculate close rate one of two wrong ways — and both hide exactly where the real problem is.
body:
Close rate sounds like a simple number: how many deals you closed, divided by how many opportunities you had. In practice, it's one of the most commonly miscalculated numbers in remodeling sales, and the way it's usually calculated hides the exact problem it's supposed to reveal.

There are two common mistakes, and they pull in opposite directions.

**Mistake 1: Calculating close rate against total leads**

If you divide jobs closed by total leads that came in, you'll get a number that looks alarmingly low — often somewhere in the single digits. That's because this calculation lumps together everyone: tire-kickers, wrong-fit inquiries, people who never responded, and genuinely qualified prospects, all treated as equally "in the running." A low number here doesn't necessarily mean your sales process is broken. It might just mean your top-of-funnel is unfiltered.

**Mistake 2: Calculating close rate against appointments only, without separating no-shows**

The opposite mistake is calculating close rate only against appointments that actually happened, which quietly excludes no-shows from the math entirely. This makes your close rate look better than it really is, and — more importantly — it hides a no-show problem that might be costing you more revenue than your actual close rate.

**The calculation that actually tells you something useful**

Close rate is most useful when it's calculated against *qualified, appointment-attending* prospects — the people who were a legitimate fit and actually showed up for the conversation. That formula looks like this:

Jobs Closed ÷ (Qualified Leads × Appointment Rate) = True Close Rate

This isolates the one thing your sales process is actually responsible for: converting a real conversation into a signed contract. Everything upstream of that — lead quality, qualification, show-up rate — gets measured separately, so you're not blaming your sales process for a lead-generation or scheduling problem, or vice versa.

**A worked example**

Say you had 120 leads last month. 55% were qualified (66 leads). Of those, 65% booked and attended an appointment (about 43 appointments). If you closed 11 jobs, your true close rate is 11 ÷ 43, or about 25.6% — not 11 ÷ 120 (9%), and not artificially inflated by excluding no-shows from the denominator.

That 25.6% is the number worth tracking month over month, because it's the one number that actually reflects how well your sales conversations are going, independent of everything else in the funnel.

**Why this distinction matters more than it seems**

If you're using the wrong version of this number, you can end up solving the wrong problem entirely. An owner who thinks their close rate is 9% might invest in sales training or a new pitch deck, when the real issue was a weak qualification process letting unqualified leads through. An owner who thinks their close rate is a healthy 40% (by excluding no-shows) might miss an appointment problem that's quietly costing them tens of thousands a month.

Once you're calculating it correctly, the same principle from our pipeline calculator applies: a five-point improvement in this specific number compounds against every lead you're already paying for, every month, without spending anything more on generating new ones. It's worth getting the number right before deciding what to fix.
